ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Projects for Development of NER 
*201. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the Minister of DEVELOPMENT OF 
NORTH EASTERN REGION be pleased to state: 
(a) the development projects in the North Eastern Region sanctioned 
by Government during 2003-04,2004-05 and 2005-06; 
(b) the funds allotted for each proj ect, the date of commencement of 
work and likely date of completion in each case; and 
(c) the steps taken/proposed to be taken to expedite the completion of 
the projects where the progress of work has been delayed for more than a 
year beyond the stipulated date? 
THE MINISTER OF DEVELOPMENT OF NORTH EASTERN REGION 
(SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) and (b) A statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. (See below). 
(c) The projects are implemented by the State Governments. None of the 
projects sanctioned in 2003-04,2004-05 & 2005-06 and already started has yet 
exceeded the stipulated time-limit.

Statement 
(a) According to the information received from the Directorates of

industries registered upto 31 Ma rch 2001 were found closed during 
enumeration.

technology, difficulty in availability of working capital and raw materials, 
constraints in electricity supply a nd other infrastructure, management 
inadequacies, etc., are some of the main reasons of closure of these units.

Statement 
Enhancement of the Foreign Direct Investment ceiling from 49 percent to 74 
per cent in the Telecom sector 
Government of India 
Ministry of Commerce and Industry 
Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion 
Secretariat for Industrial Assistance 
PRESS NOTE No. 5 (2005 SERIES) 
1 Jn pursuance of the Government's commitment to liberalise the FDI regime, 
it has been decided to enhance the Foreign Direct Investment ceiling from 49 
per cent to 74 per cent in certain telecom services [such as Basic, Cellular, 
Unified Access Service, National/International Long Distance, V-Sat, Public 
Mobile  Radio Trunked Services (PMRTS), Global Mobile Personal 
Communications Services (GMPCS) ana other value added services], subject to the 
following conditions:— 
A. The total composite foreign holding including but not limited to 
investments by Foreign Institutional Investors (Flls), Non-Resident 
Indians (NRIs), Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs), 
American Depository Receipts (ADRs), Global Depository 
Receipts (GDRs), convertible preference shares, proportionate foreign 
investment in Indian promoters/investment companies including 
their holding companies, etc., herein after referred as FDI, will not 
exceed 74 per cent. This, 74 per cent foreign investment can be 
made directly or indirectly in the operating company or through a 
holding company. Hence, the remaining 26 per cent will be owned by 
resident Indian citizens or an Indian Company (i.e. foreign direct 
investment does not exceed 49 per cent and the management is with the 
Indian owners). It is clarified that proportionate foreign component of 
such an Indian Company will also be counted towards the ceiling of 74 
per cent. However, foreign component in the total holding of Indian 
public sector banks and Indian public sector financial institutions will be 
treated as 'Indian' holding. The lincensee will be required to disclose the 
status of such foreign holding and certify that the foreign 
investment is within the ceiling of 74 per cent on a half yearly 
basis.

[6 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
B. The majority Directors on the Board including Chairman, 
Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) shall be 
resident Indian citizens, enforced through licence agreement. 
The appointment to these positions from among resident Indian 
citizens shall be made in consultation with serious Indian 
investors. Serious investor has been defined below in para G (ii). 
C. The share Holder Agreements (S HA) shall specifically incorporate

Report of Expert Group for review of IT Act 
1362. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will th e Minister of COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the expert group constituted for an indepth review of issues relating 
to Information Technology Act, 2000 have submitted its report; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what action has been taken on the recommendations, so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) The summary of the recommendations of the Expert Committee is given 
in the enclosed statement (see below). 
(c) The recommendations of the Expert committee has been deliberated at 
length in the Ministry and the Draft Cabinet Note has been prepared based on 
the recommendations. Draft Cabinet Note has already been circulated for 
inter-ministerial consultations. 
Statement 
Summary of the recommendations of the Expert Committee 
1. As the technologies and applications in IT sector change very rapidly, some 
of the provisions related to parameters that may change from time to time have 
been suggested to provide for the new developments to be corporated by 
changes in rules/govt. notifications. This would enable the law to be amended and 
approved much faster and would keep our laws in line with the changing 
technological environment. 
2. In view of changing needs, operation of the Sub-section 4 of Section 1 may 
be made more flexible through prescription of such exception by rules rather 
than being part of the main Act. 
3. The Committee has restructed several provisions in relation to 
recognition of Digital signatures, e-governance, penalties and adjudication. 
The suggestion is to make the Information Technology Act technically 
natural with minimum change in the IT Act, 2000. The amendment have 
been suggested in Section 4 of the Act to provide for electronic signature. 
115 

RAJYASABHA [6 March, 2006]  
With digital signature as one of the types of electronic signature and by 
enabling the detail of other form of electronic signature to be provided in the 
rules to be notified by the Central Government from time to time. This is enabling 
provision for Central Government to exercise as to when the technology other 
than digital signature matures. 
4. The Committee has revisited Section 43, 65, 66, 67, 72 and 79 to focus 
issues pertaining to data protection and privacy so as to enable healthy 
business environment. The stringent provisions have been suggested in the 
Section. Proposals at Section 43(ii) related to enabling of sensitive personnel with 
reasonable security proposals and procedures thereto have been recommended. The 
amendments have been suggested in Section 72 pertaining to breach of 
confidentiality and privacy. A new Sub-section as 72(H) has been suggested to 
prevent intermidiaries to disclose information relating to user without his 
consent. 
5. The Section 72 pertaining to breach  of confidentiality have been 
redefined. The report of the Expert Committee seeks to address the new 
phenomenon of video voyeurism, including transmission of MMS clips, the 
images of private areas of indi viduals without knowledge and its 
transmission without their consent.  The new sub-Section has been 
proposed in Section 72 of the IT Act, 2000. 
6. Amendment have been recommended in Section 69 of the IT Act, 2000 
relating to the power to issue protection for inspection and monitoring any 
information through computer resource to take care of the concerns expressed 
by Ministry of Home Affairs. 
 
7. In line with the Indian Penal Code, the Expert Committee has 
advocated classifications of Cyber Laws in cognizable and non-cognizable 
accordingly. Language of Section 66 related to computer related offences may be 
revised to be in lines with Section 43 related to penalty for damage to computer 
resource. These have been graded with less degree of severity of offence when done 
by any person, dishonestly or fraudulently without the permission of the 
owner. 
8. Section 67 related to Obscenity in electronic form has been revised to bring 
in line with IPC and other laws but fine has been increased because of ease of such 
operation in electronic form; link up with Section 79 w.r.t. liability of 
intermediary in certain cases has been provided. 
9. Anew section 67(2) has been suggested to address child pornography with 
higher punishment, a globally accepted offence. 
116 

[6 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
10. A new Section 68(1) has been proposed for providing modes and 
methods for encryption for secure use of the electronic medium, as 
recommended by earlir Inter Ministerial Working Group on Cyber Laws & 
Cyber Forensics (IMWG) 
11. A new section 78 A (Examiners of Electronic Evidence) may be added 
to notify the examiners of  electronic evidence by the Central Government. 
This will help the Judiciary/Adjudicating officers in handling technical issues. 
12. Section 79 has been revised to bring-out explicitly the extent of liability 
of intermediary in certain cases. EU Directive on E-Commerce 2000/31/EC 
issued on June 8th 2000 has been used as guiding principles. Power to make rules 
w.r.t. the functioning of the "Intermediary" including "Cyber Cafes" has been 
provided for under Section 87.

1373. SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: W ill the Minister of 
DEVELOPMENT OF NORTH EASTERN REGION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is  delay in clearing of the projects 
submitted by the North Eastern States under NLCPR to the DoNER affect the 
projects at the implementation State: 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what steps Government have taken to remove the bureaucratic red tapism 
to ensure speedy clearance of the schemes submitted by the North Eastern 
States? 
THE MINISTER OF DEVELOPMENT OF NORTH EASTERN REGION 
(SHRI PR. KYNDIAH): (a) to (c) Delay is  not caused in clearing projects 
submitted by the North Eastern State und er Non-Lapsable Central Pool of 
Resources (NLCPR) to the Ministry of Development of North Eastern 
Region. However, some delay is caused by State Governments in submission 
of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) and also in submission of revised DPRs after 
the expert comments of relevant Central Ministries, on the original DPRs, are 
conveyed to them. In order to facilitate early clearance of projects we keep on 
pursuing with the concerned State Governments for early submission of 
DPRs/Revised DPRs.

Right to education as a fundamental right 
1380. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI:  
        SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have recognised the right to education as a 
Fundamental Right of the citizen by inserting Article 21A in Part III of the 
Constitution; 
(b) if so, since when; 
(c) whether necessary legislative measures have been enacted in this regard; 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; 
(e) by when the necessary legislation in this regard could be expected; 
(f) whether Government are facing fiscal snag; and 
(g) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (g) The 
Constitution (86th Amendment) Act, 2002, which came into force on 13th 
December 2002, seeks to make free and compulsory education a 
Fundamental Right for all children in the age-group 6-14 years by inserting a new 
Article 21-Ain Part III ("Fundamental Right") of the Constitution. 
Based on the report of a committee set up by the reconstituted Central Advisory 
Board of Education (CABE) to suggest a draft of the legislation envisaged under 
Article 21A, a draft Right to Education Bill 2005 was prepared and sent to all 
State Governments/UTs and Central Ministries for their views. 
In the meanwhile, the Prime Minister also constituted and small group 
comprising Minister of Human Resource Development, Finance Minister, Deputy 
Chairman, Planning Commission and Chairman of the PM's Economic 
Advisory Council to examine, inter-alia, the legal, constitutional and financial 
implications of the Bill. The meeting of this group has been held and the 
report received.

Parameters for according classical language status 
1381. SHRI K. B. KRISHNAMURT HY: Will the Ministrer of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the parameters prescribed for according classical language status; 
(b) the languages so far that have fulfilled all the conditions and have been 
accorded classical language status; 
(c) whether Karnataka Government has requested to accord classical 
language status to Kannada language; and 
(d) if so, the present status of the above proposal? 
THE M!NISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) The following criteria 
was laid down by the Ministry of Home Affairs to determine the eligibility of 
languages to be considered for classification as a 'Classical Language'. 
(i) High antiquity of its early texts/recorded history over a period of 
1500-2000 years, (ii) A body of ancient literature/texts, which is 
considered a valuable 
heritage by generations of speakers; (iii) The literary tradition be 
original and not borrowed from another 
speech community; and (iv) The classical language and literature 
being distinct from modern, 
there may also be a discontinuity between the Classical 
Language and its later forms or its offshoots. 
(b) Sanskrit and Tamil. 
(c) and (d) Ministry of Culture has r eceived representations from various 
quarters for declaring Kannada as classical language. A Committee of 
Linguistic Experts has been constituted to examine the claims of any Indian 
Language for Classical Status. This Committee will advise the Government in 
the matter.

other facilities for their students; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (c) National 
Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) constituted 21 Focus 
Groups in November 2004 including a Focus Group on "Art, Music, Dance and 
Theatre", with the aim to produce research based position papers providing a 
comprehensive review of existing knowledge and representing an awareness 
of the field reality, specially in rural schools. The main objective of production 
of research based position papers was to provide an accessible resource to 
curriculum designers and writers of textbooks and other materials including 
teacher guides. 
The Focus Group on "Art, Music, Dance & Theatre", has concluded that the 
inclusion of art education in the curriculum of school education has certain 
important objectives apart from contributing significantly to the overall 
development of the child's personality. At pre-primary stage, all subjects 
should be taught through drawing, painting, clay modeling, role-play, dance, 
story telling, singing etc. At primary stage, the orientation should be towards 
art as a medium of self-expression. At upper primary & secondary stages, need 
is to aim at developing learner's awareness and interest in a wide variety of 
arts. At higher secondary stage, art education should be treated as a specialized 
subject.

the standards of newspapers and news agencies in India and to inculcate 
principles of self-regulation among the press. The Government follows a policy of 
non-interference in the functioning of the Council and it enjoys complete 
autonomy in its functioning. The Council, which is in the nature of a self-
regulatory body of the Press, has built "Norms of Journalistic Conduct", which

Anganwadis as focal point for health care activity 
1462. MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR : Will the Minister of WOMEN 
AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to make Anganwadis the focal point of all 
mother and child-related health care activity; 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [6 March, 2006] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government propose to integrate different services to control high 
maternal and child mortality in the country, especially with reference to Orissa 
State; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and 
(b) Anganwadi Centre is the focal point of delivery of services under the 
Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme which is Centrally-
sponsored scheme implemented through the States/UTs. The services 
provided to children below 6 years and pregnant & lactating mothers through 
Anganwadi Centres are supplementary nutrition, immunization, referral 
services, health check-up, pre-school non-formal education and nutrition & 
health education. Health-related services viz. Immunization, Health check-up 
and Referral services are delivered through the public health infrastructure i.e. 
Health Sub-centre, Primary Health Centres & Community Health Centres. 
(c) and (d) The ICDS Scheme envisa ges inter-sectoral convergence with 
health schemes/programmes. The Government of India, Ministry of Health & 
Family Welfare has launched National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) to 
improve the availability and access to quality health care including immunization & 
safe motherhood with special focus on States having weak health indicators. The 
State of Orissa is covered under NRHM. The Reproductive and Child Health 
(RCH) Programme remains one of the major thrusts of the NRHM and a new 
initiative viz. Integrated Management of Neo-natal & Childhood Illness 
(IMNCI) would also be implemented, in a phased manner, under RCH-II. 
The areas of convergence under NRHM include ante-natal, post-natal check-
up and family planning counseling; child health services facilitate referral to 
appropriate health facilities, particularly institutional deliveries, RTI/STI etc. 
All these measures are expected to have a significant effect on controlling high 
maternal and child mortality in the country, including Orissa.

Non-compliance of SC order regarding sexual harassment 
1465. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a recently published report of National Commission on 
Women which covered 799 organizations including Government Departments 
has revealed that there is poor compliance of Supreme Court order with regard to 
sexual harassment of women at work place; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action Government have taken or propose to take against the persons 
for violating the Supreme Court order? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) National 
Commission for Women (NCW) has informed that it had held interactive 
meetings on sexual harassment at work place since November, 2000 with 799 
organizations. It was observed that 664 organizations were having Complaint 
Committee. 414 organizations reported third party involvement in the Complaints 
Committee set up by them. According to NCW it would not be correct to say 
that there is poor compliance with the Supreme Court guidelines. However, the 
guidelines have not been fully followed in as much as complaint Committee 
has not been set up by many organizations, the Complaint Committees which 
have been set up do not have 50% reservation for women and are headed in some 
cases by men, many do not have third party representation and there is noticeable 
lack of awareness among Complaints Committee members. 
(c) The Government has taken a number of initiatives to promote 
compliance with the Supreme Court guidelines. The details are enclosed as 
Statement (See below). NCW has also since proposed a draft bill on the 
prevention of sexual harassment of women at workplace, incorporating the 
Supreme Court guidelines. 
244 

[6 March, 2006]   RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
Details of steps taken by the Government to implement the guidelines 
laid down by the Supreme Court and to create awareness about the 
issue of sexual harassment at workplace 
' The Government has requested all the Central Ministries/ 
Departments, Chief Secretaries of all the State Governments/Union 
Territory Administrations, Universities/Institutions, Central Board of 
Secondary Education, All India Co uncil of Technical Education to 
constitute complaints committees and to ensure that the guidelines 
laid down by the Supreme Court in the Vishaka case for prevention of 
sexual harassment at work place are implemented. 
• The National Commission for Women (NCW) formulated a Code of 
Conduct for Workplace, puttin g down the Supreme Court's 
guidelines mentioned above in a simple manner. This has been 
circulated to State Commissions for Women, Non-Govemmental 
Organisations, the apex bodies of the Corporate Sector, Public Sector 
Undertakings, Media, Ministries/Departments and other institutions. 
• The NCW has instituted a series of interactive meetings with Public Sector 
Undertakings/Banks/Universities/Educational Institutions/ 
Hotels/Media etc. to assess the extent of implementation of the 
guidelines. 
• Department of Public Enterprises issued circular in May, 1998 to all 
administrative Ministries/Departments concerned with Central Public 
Sector Establishments to direct the Chief Executives of CPSEs under 
their administrative control for adherence and compliance of the 
Supreme Court's guidelines on prevention of sexual harassment by making 
amendments in the CDA Rules of CPSEs. 
• A Central Committee headed by Secretary, Department of Women and 
Child Development has been constituted in the Department of Women 
and Child Development to review the implementation of the guidelines. 
During the year 2004, the Committee met on 27-7-2004. In pursuance 
of the meeting, all Ministries/Departments and State Governments/UT 
Administrations were again requested to ensure setting up of complaints 
committee and to ensure its proper functioning. 
• So far as implementation of the Supreme Court guidelines in regard to 
setting up of complaint committee in small establishments like shops 
and call centres are concerned, section 1 (3) of the Industrial 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [6 March, 2006] 
Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1947 applies to every 
establishment wherein 100 and more workers are employed. 
However, appropriate Government may apply the provisions of the Act to 
any industrial establishment employing less than 100 persons. Since 
the State Govenment are the appropriate Government in respect of 
commercial establishments like shops and call centres, necessary 
instruction have been issued by the Ministry of Labour and 
Employment during January, 2005 to all Labour Secretaries asking 
them to suitable action to apply the provisions of the Industrial 
Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 to small establishments like 
call centres and shops in the unorganised sector. 
• The Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964 have been 
amended to include sexual harassment as a misconduct. The Central 
Civil Services (Control, Classification and Appeal) Rules, 1965 have 
been amended during July, 2004 to provide that the complaints 
Committee established in each Ministry or Department or office for 
inquiring into complaints of sexual harassment shall be deemed to be 
the inquiry authority appointed by the disciplinary authority and 
complaints committee shall hold the inquiry as far as practicable in 
accordance with the procedure laid down in these rules (i.e. the 
procedure for holding inquiry into disciplinary proceedings for 
award of a major penality). 
• Amendments have been made to Industrial Employment (Standing 
Orders) Act, 1946 so that the sexual harassment of women at 
workplace in the private sector could constitute an offence for which 
a workman is liable for disciplinary action. 
• Necessary instruction have been issued by the Ministry of Labour and 
Employment during January, 2005 to all State Labour Secretaries 
asking them to take suitable action to apply the provisions of the 
Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 to small 
establishments like call centres and shops in the unorganised sector. 
• Media compaign has been undertaken by the Department of Women 
and Child Development to create awareness on various issues 
concerning women and children, including compliance with the Supreme 
Court's guidelines on the prevention of sexual harassment of women 
at workplace. 
Malnutrition among children 
1466. SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
246 

[6 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether it is a fact that in spite of Government initiative and various 
measures such as National Nutrition Policy, National Plan of Action for 
Nutrition, etc. one in every three malnourished children in the world, 
according to the UNICEF publication en titled, 'Mapping India's Children: 
UNICEF in action' lives in India; and 
(b) if so, the reason for which the malnourishment in the Indian Children has 
not been reduced? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) Yes, Madam. 
UNICEF Publication under reference reports so. There has, however, been a 
significant reduction in the prevalence of under-nutrition among children, clinical 
symptoms of Vitamin A Deficiency, Iron  Deficiency and I odine Deficiency 
Disorders during the last three decades. 
(b) Malnutrition is maltifaceted problem. The determinants of malnutrition vary 
from female illiteracy, poor purchasing" power, food insecurity and inadequate 
access to basic social services like Health, Education, Welfare, etc. The prevention 
and control of malnutrition, therefore, requires a multisectoral and multi-
dimensional approach. The Government of India is seized of the problem and has 
been implementing a number of direct and indirect interventions through its 
different sectors which aim at improving nutritional status of the population. Some 
of these include Integrated Child Development Service (ICDS) Scheme, Kishori 
Shakti Yojana (KSY), Nutrition Programme for Adolescent Girls (NPAG). 
Nutrition Advocacy and Awareness Generation Programmes of Food and Nutrition 
Board (FNB) of the Ministry of Women & Child Development, Mid Day Meal 
Programme for primary school children of the Department of Elementary 
Education and Literacy, Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS), Antodaya 
Anna Yojna (AAY), Anapurna Scheme of the Department of Food and Public 
Distribution. Reproductive and Child Health Programme, National Iodine 
Deficiency Disorders Control Program me, National Rural Health Mission, 
Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness of Ministry of Health 
and Family Welfare, various poverty alleviation and food for work programmes 
of Ministry of Rural Development, public health measures like vaccination, de-
worming, supply of safe drinking water and sanitation also contribute to 
improving macro (Energy and Protein) and micronutrient (Vitamins and 
Minerals) status of the population in different ways.

Share of women in total workforce 
1468. SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the share of women in total workforce; and 
(b) the steps being taken to augment their share? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) As 
per the census of India 2001 data, female workers account for 31.63% share of 
the total workers in India. 
(b) The Government has taken various steps to augment the share of women 
in the total workeforce. These include: 
Programmes and institutional support for skill development and capacity 
building: 
Ministry of Women and Child Development has been implementing the 
schemes: Support to Training and Employment Programme and 
Swawlamban, to provide training and skills to women to facilitate them to obtain 
employment or self employment on a sustainable basis. 
248 

[6 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Another programme being implemented by the Ministry of Women and Child 
Development, namely, Swayamsidha, aims at holistic empowerment of women 
through, among other things, economic empowerment and convergence of 
various schemes. 
To give special focus on the skill training development of women, the 
Directorate General of Employment & Training (DGE&T) under the Ministry of 
Labour & Employment has set up a Women's Training Directorate which aims at 
promoting participation of women in skill training. Under the Women's 
Vocational Training programmes, institutionalized skill training is being offered 
to women in basic, advanced & post-advanced skills for improving the 
employability of women in wage/self-employment. In the State Sector, a 
network of exclusive Women Industrial Training Institutes (WITIs) have been 
set up under the administrative control of the State Governments. 
Special provision for reservation for women: 
The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 stipulates that at least 
one third of the beneficiaries of the schemes implemented under Act shall be 
women. 
Some State Governments such as  Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Maharashtra, Orissa, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu have schemes of reservation 
for women in Government service. 
Creating a positive and congenial work environment for women workers: 
A number of protective provisions favouring women have been 
incorporated in the various labour laws such as Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, 
the Factories Act, 1948, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, 
the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 etc. 
Assistance to women job seekers: 
The Employment Exchange take special care to cater to the job needs of 
women registered with them.

Sir, let me recapitulate the essential facts of the matter. Iran has a legal 
right to develop peaceful uses of nuclear energy, but it has also certain 
obligations and respon sibilities based on the ex istence of several 
unanswered question that Iran agreed to start the process of assisting the 
Intenational Atomic Energy Agency with investigation into several past 
activities of its nuclear programme. An important part of this process was 
voluntary suspension by Iran of all enrichment and reprocessing activity in 
Novemeber2004. However, since last August, Iran has renewed production 
of Uranium Hexafluroide, and since then, of uranium enrichment. Unresolved 
question regarding centrifuge imports and designs to make uranium metallic 
hemispheres remain. The origin of such procurement is an issue of direct 
concern for us. 
Under these circumstances, our position was based on these facts, 
which emerged from an objective ivestigation by the International Atomic 
Energy Agency, and through information disclosed by Iran itself. 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, there is also the question that several hon. 
Members raised regarding the International Atomic Energy Agency Board 
of Governor's meeting today. I should inform Members that it is as yet not 
clear in what manner this issue will be taken up by the Board of Governors 
today. The Resolution adopted by the Board of Governors last month 
mentions certain steps that Iran and the International Atomic Energy Agency 
will be taking. Discussions are taking place in Vienna on this matter. The 
Government's approach will be based on our consistent policy of promoting 
efforts for a resolution of issues through dialogue and discussions. I would 
like to assure the hon. Members that Government will take into account 
the sentiments expressed in this House in this context. 
Some points were also made, including Shri Yechuri, regarding options 
that could have been explored by India and the International community. 
There have been discussions between Iran and Russia in this regard. We 
remain hopeful that solutions acceptable to all sides will be found. We do 
not favour confrontation,  rhetoric or coercive measures as these only 
exacerbate tensions in the region and beyond. India has consistently stated 
that all sides must work to find mutually acceptable compromise solutions, 
and that confrontation should be avoided at all costs. For this to be possible, 
time must be given for diplomacy to work. I think Sir there is consensus in 
Parliament and in our country that confrontation is not in the interests of

Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, several hon. Members, including Shrimati Sushma 
Swaraj, expressed worries regarding our relations with Iran, and the effect of 
these developments on this important relationship. Sir, as I said in my suo 
motu statement, our Government is committed to widening, deepening and 
expanding our diverse and mutually beneficial ties with Iran. Only recently, 
my colleague, the Minister of State for External Affairs, Shri E. Ahammed,

Republic of Iran. Shri Ahammed emphasized our desire to remain engaged

Sir, Government will continue to monitor the situation closely and will

In dealing with this issue, we will pay due attention to our relationship 
with Iran, the need to maintain peace and stability in the Gulf region and 
safeguarding our own security. 
Sir, I reiterate that this House can rest assured that we will also take

Death of Birds' in Okhla Sanctuary, Delhi 
SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN (Uttar Pradesh): Sir, 53 migratory birds 
were found dead in Okhla Bird Sanctuary, Delhi, earlier this month. Later, 
three fishermen were arrested for adding poison to the water body. It 
has now been revealed in a report given by the Wildlife Departments of 
U.R and Delhi that the deaths were due to the polluted Yamuna water. 
The reports have also sounded an alarm that more such deaths 
cannot be ruled out till the polluted water in the sanctuary is cleared. 
Sir, I would therefore, demand from the Government that the fishermen 
who have been proved innocent be released forthwith. 
The report prepared by Delhi's conservator of Forests has 
indicated that the problem plauguing the Sanctuary is the presence of 
toxic pollutants in water. The water is unfit for any use. 
The Sanctuary consists of wetlands and water body formed by 
Kalindi barrage on the Yamuna. Thejvetland attracts large number of 
migratory birds. While the U.R Govemment has declared the area falling 
in its territory as a wild life sanctuary under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 
1972, Dehi has not done so on its part. 
The Yamuna river water is polluted not only in this area but the river 
as a whole is extremely polluted because of the discharge from 
industries as well as domestic households. This needs to be addressed 
immediately. Secondly, Delhi has become unfit to receive migratory 
birds because of the quality of water. Mere forests will not attract the 
birds unless water quality is improved. 
I request the Govemment to act immediately.

Plight of Silk Fabric and Handloom Weavers 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Sir, I rise to draw the urgent attention 
of this House and also the Government to the sorrows and sufferings of 
the silk fabric weavers of Uttar Pradesh, more so of Banaras. 
To meet their demand of silk yarn, they are dependant on imported 
goods from China. The price of such yarn has increased by about 60 per 
cent during the past two to three years from 18 to 22 dollars a kilogram to 
22 to 35 dollars. This is due to increase in import duty and other taxes. 
Import of finished fabric also has po sed not only competition, but also 
threat to the domestic weavers. 
During the past few years, 60 to 80 per cent of handloom units have 
closed down. People, who are traditionally engaged and employed in these 
industry have migrated or are living in poverty. Rise in electricity tariff, 
irregular supply of electricity, lack of banking and marketing facilities are 
other reasons for the dwindling of this age-old traditional craft. 
I am afraid, Sir, the day is not far away when the indian silk industry will 
become totally extinct. Thus, a glorious  tradition of Indian silk art and 
fabric craft will vanish. 
Therefore, it is time for the Government to consider and evolve an integrated 
policy to help and support the traditional weavers. Like farmers and other 
artisans, they need subsidy in power tariff, cut in import duty, better marketing 
facilities, insurance cover and socio-economic rehabilitation. 
Through these measures only the trade and commerce of the silk fabric 
industry can service and grow. I urge upon the Government, more so the 
hon. Minister of Textiles, to attend to these issues urgently. 
Thank you. 
Demand for a concerted approach towards Rural 
Telecommunication Connectivity 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA(Maharashtra): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, although 
various policy initiatives have been taken by the Government, particularly 
setting up of the universal service obligation funds (USOF), the growth of rural 
teledensity has remained insignificant and the gap between urban and rural 
276 

[6 March, 2006] RAJYASABHA 
teledensity is widening—presently 31 per cent and 1.94 per cent respectively. 
It is a clear evidence that existing approach of USOF to fund PCOs and 
individual rural telephone connections has not been successful to the extent 
envisaged in increasing teledensity. The approach seems to be based on the 
premise that build-up of infrastructure will be far more effective in making 
telecommunication facilities available in large numbers in rural areas in a 
manner similar to urban areas, rather than funding of individual telephones. 
Since the growth in telecome service is taking place through mobile service, 
the scope of USOF cannot be limited to fixed services only. In fact, the National 
Telecom Policy (NTP), 1999 did mention that in addition to fixed service 
providers, other service providers could also be encouraged to participate in 
USO provisions, of course, subject to technical feasibility and can.be 
reimbursed from the funds of Universal Access Levy. TRAI's two-pronged 
approach, while giving recommendations on the growth of telecommunication 
facilities in rural (i) relaying on mobile communciation system and (ii) based 
on provisioning of broadband type of connectivity, need to be seriously 
considered i the context of USOF so that a beginning could be made towards 
substantially increasing the present abysmal low rural density from 1.94 per 
cent to at least 5 per cent in a foreseeable future.

SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHERJEE (Assam): Sir, before 1996 about

as the expenditure on workers' salary and maintenance was a continuous 
process without production. Realizing the pathetic condition of the industry, 
the Governments of Assam and Arunchal Pradesh requested the Central 
Government for extending benefits of various exemptions under the North-
Eastern Industry Policy, 1997, to this industry. A Notification of additional
